subtitulo: Getting served at a Spanish counter in one short sentence — and knowing what the counter, the table and the terrace each cost before you choose one
cena: Ten to two, the bar is three deep, the barman looks at you, says '¡Dime!', and gives you about a second and a half before he moves on.

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you those sentences. You made them on the spot, out of two openers you now own.
clique.piso: You will be served in one short sentence, with no 'sorry' in front of it. Most visitors spend a fortnight waiting to be noticed.

frasePiso: You will be served in one short sentence, with no 'sorry' in front of it. Most visitors spend a fortnight waiting to be noticed.
permissao: You are allowed to stand at a counter with one small beer for an hour, and you are allowed to ask what the terrace costs before you sit in it. Both are ordinary. And when you cannot name the thing you want, point at it — the frame carries the rest of the sentence for you.
espelho: Waiting quietly to be noticed is the bit that reads as odd there. At a Spanish counter, saying nothing is read as not being ready yet, and the barman moves along.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The barman says '¡Dime!', looks straight at you, and gives you about a second and a half before his eyes move down the bar.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: He is being brusque with me, and I am about to be rushed into ordering something I have not decided on.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: It is the handover, not the pressure. At a busy counter the attention goes to one customer at a time and moves on the moment it is not used; '¡Dime!' is him passing it to you.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Look up, hold his eye, and say the order in one short sentence, louder than feels polite. No greeting run-up, no apology in front.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You are served on the first pass of his attention instead of the fourth, and you have the volume of the room right for the rest of the fortnight.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a hotel breakfast counter, where they will wait as long as you like — the clock here is a bar clock, not a Spanish clock.

fichasCulturais.sinal: There is a printed list by the door with the same drink written on it two or three times, at two or three amounts.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They keep two sets of prices and I am about to be given the tourist one.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The counter, the indoor table and the terrace are each allowed their own amount, and the displayed list is what the law asks for in exchange — it has to be visible and the amount on it already includes tax.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Read it for four seconds before you choose where to put yourself, or ask out loud whether the counter is the same.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You pick your seat knowing what the seat costs, and the difference over a fortnight quietly buys the last round of the holiday.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a one-room bar with four stools and no terrace — where there is nowhere else to sit there is one amount, and asking makes you look like you are auditing them.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A small plate you did not order lands next to your drink.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: Either this is the famous free tapa, or it is going quietly onto the bill and I will find out at the end.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The plate with the round is a regional habit rather than a national rule: in eastern Andalusia, and Granada above all, it comes with the drink; in Barcelona, Madrid, San Sebastián and Valencia it is an item you are buying.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask once, on the first round, whether it comes with the drink — before you eat it and before anyone adds anything up.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: In Granada you order the second round knowing a different plate is coming with it, which is the best deal in the country.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a Basque pintxo bar: there you help yourself from the counter and the sticks left on your plate are what you are billed for, so you keep every one of them.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Since 2022 hospitality venues in Spain have had to always offer customers unpackaged water free of charge — in practice, tap water on request.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: A bar may charge different amounts at the counter, at an indoor table and on the terrace, but it has to state that on a displayed price list, and the amount shown is final, with tax already included.

steps.pt: Warm-up, ten seconds. Flat palm: ca-ña. ba-rra. te-rra-za. Hold each vowel. If the hand tilts, the vowel slid.

steps.promptPt: The bar door has SOLO EFECTIVO taped to it, and your wallet holds a card and nothing else. Ask the man on the step for the thing that fixes that. Speak now.
steps.pt: somewhere to get money out
Ten to two on a Tuesday. The bar is three deep, the counter is wet, and you are two rows back.
His eyes come along the row and land on you. He says one word, and you have about a second and a half.
👂 'Go on.' — that is him handing you the counter.
👂 'Whose turn?' — answer, or the person behind you will.
👂 'What are you two having?' — you will hear it daily and never have to say it.
Any of those three means you. Look up, hold his eye, and say it a little louder than feels polite.
Here is the frame that gets you served, and it is three words long. ¿Me pones — and then the thing.

steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs OO-nah KAH-nyah, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: A small draught beer, please.
The front never moves. The thing on the end is the only part that ever changes. Listen to him again.

steps.es: ¿Me pones un café con leche, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs oon kah-FEH kon LEH-cheh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: A white coffee, please.
steps.tts: ¿Me pones un café con leche, por favor?

steps.pt: One word to bank: caña. A small glass of draught. Ask for 'a beer' in English and a pricey bottle arrives.

steps.promptPt: Half eleven, a neighbourhood bar, and every hand along the counter is holding the same short cold glass. He has just said your word. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs OO-nah KAH-nyah, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: the short glass everyone has

steps.promptPt: Out on the terrace now, in the sun, and you are not drinking alone — the person opposite wants exactly what you want. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs dohs KAH-nyahs, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: make it a pair

steps.promptPt: Quarter past eight, the station bar, your train in twenty minutes, and beer is a step too far. Order what the man beside you is having with his toast. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me pones un café con leche, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs oon kah-FEH kon LEH-cheh, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: the breakfast one, with milk
It is not only drinks. Thirty-six degrees, two of you, and a bottle nobody asked for is heading your way.
Since 2022 every bar and restaurant here has to offer unpackaged water free. Five words collect it.
Tap water, please. ('grifo' is the tap)
The same frame takes it, and you can ask for enough to fill the table. One trip for him, and no bottle.

steps.encaixe: una jarra de agua del grifo
steps.promptPt: Two of you at an outside table, thirty-six degrees, and he is already walking to the fridge for a bottle you would be paying for. Head him off. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me pones una jarra de agua del grifo?
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs OO-nah KHAH-rrah deh AH-gwah del GREE-foh
steps.pt: the free one, and enough of it
steps.tts: ¿Me pones una jarra de agua del grifo?

steps.pt: On a tourist street you will sometimes hear 'sorry, bottled only'. You do not argue. One calm line does it.
It's free by law, isn't it?

steps.promptPt: 'Sorry, we only do bottled.' You are still smiling and still sitting down. Remind him what the rule is, as a question. Speak now.
steps.pt: the polite reminder

steps.es: Sí, sí. Ahora os traigo una jarra.
steps.pinyin: see, see. ah-OH-rah ohs TRAI-goh OO-nah KHAH-rrah
steps.pt: 👂 'Yes, of course. I'll bring you a jug.' — that is where it ends, nearly every time.
steps.tts: Sí, sí. Ahora os traigo una jarra.

steps.pt: Most of the time the jug simply appears. And if it truly does not, that is a job for a form we meet later.
And this is not a crusade. If you would rather have a cold bottle, have a cold bottle — nobody is counting.

steps.es: Una botella de agua sin gas, por favor.
steps.pinyin: OO-nah boh-TEH-yah deh AH-gwah seen gahs, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: 👂 A bottle of still water, please. 'Sin gas' is still and 'con gas' is fizzy — the English word 'still' gets you nowhere.
steps.tts: Una botella de agua sin gas, por favor.

steps.pt: Bread lands without being ordered and, in most of Spain, goes onto the bill. Legal, if it is on the list.
Is the bread charged separately?

steps.promptPt: A basket nobody asked for is sitting between you, still untouched, and the waiter is walking away. Stop him and find out what it will cost. Speak now.
steps.pt: is it on the bill
We don't want bread, thanks. (send it back untouched — nobody minds)
Now the list by the door that almost nobody reads. The same beer on it, written two or three times.
Counter, inside table, terrace: each may cost its own amount. The list has to be visible, tax already in.

steps.es: ¿Es el mismo precio en la barra?
steps.pinyin: es el MEES-moh PREH-thyoh en lah BAH-rrah
steps.pt: Is it the same price at the counter?
steps.tts: ¿Es el mismo precio en la barra?

steps.promptPt: A pretty square in Seville, one free table in the sun, and the waiter is already pulling a chair out for you. Before you sit, find out what the sun costs. Speak now.
steps.pt: does the sun cost extra
Four seconds of reading, and the seat you take is a seat you chose. That is the whole habit.
One more from the door: if they point at a code and your phone has no signal, a paper one has to exist.

steps.es: ¿Me deja ver la carta en papel, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh DEH-khah behr lah KAR-tah en pah-PEL, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Could I see the menu on paper, please?
steps.tts: ¿Me deja ver la carta en papel, por favor?

steps.pt: A small plate you did not order arrives beside your drink. Whether it is a gift depends on the map.
Free with the round in eastern Andalusia, Granada above all. In Barcelona and Madrid it is an item you buy.

steps.promptPt: First round of the evening, and something small has landed next to your glass. Settle it now, before you eat it. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿La tapa va incluida con la bebida?
steps.pinyin: lah TAH-pah bah een-kloo-EE-dhah kon lah beh-BEE-dhah
steps.pt: is it a gift or an item
In a Basque pintxo bar it flips: you take them off the counter yourself and the sticks are the bill. Keep them.
And when you cannot tell what is inside the little plate, there is one word that opens it. You get it whole later.
Has it got ham or chorizo in it?
GUIRI ALERT. Here is your order, read back to you. 'Sorry, hello — I was wondering if I might possibly get a beer?'
Beautifully brought up. Meanwhile he has lost the thread, served three other people and forgotten you exist.
The politeness lives in your tone and one 'por favor' at the end. Not in five layers of padding out in front.
Sitting down needs two more sentences. First: is the kitchen even awake? Half seven is early in this country.
Are you serving food right now?

steps.promptPt: Ten past seven, you are starving, and there is a waiter in the doorway of a place that is lit up and empty. Ask from the pavement, before you sit for forty minutes. Speak now.
steps.pt: is the kitchen open

steps.promptPt: Inside a busy restaurant, and someone with a pile of cards under one arm is looking at you and the person beside you. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: TYEH-nen MEH-sah PAH-rah dohs — SOH-mohs dohs
steps.pt: somewhere to sit, and how many
👂 'Inside, or out on the terrace?' — the same drink is legally allowed to cost more out there. Answer on purpose.
Sitting down there is a second opener, and it works at every counter in the country. It gets its own turn next.
I'd like the menu, please.
Your glass is empty. You do not need a new sentence for that. The second frame is one word long.
Another one, please.

steps.promptPt: Back at the counter, the glass in front of you empty for a while now, and he is going past with a tray. Two words and a please. Speak now.
steps.pt: one more of the same
That is a whole sentence with nothing after it — the empty glass says the rest. Put a thing on it and it travels.
Another wine, please.
The end of the word moved with the thing hanging off it. You take that by ear, never by rule. Nobody minds.

steps.promptPt: Breakfast, the same bar, and the small cup in front of you has been empty for ten minutes. You want a second one of them. Speak now.
steps.pt: one more of these

steps.promptPt: The restaurant table, and the thing in your right hand has just gone off the edge and onto the floor. The waiter is two steps away. Speak now.
steps.pt: a clean one, please
Back to that second and a half. He is not rushing you — he is handing the counter over, and it does not wait.
Take it in one short sentence, at bar volume. Leave it lying there and it goes to the person behind you.
Not at a hotel breakfast counter, mind — there they will wait all morning. This clock is a bar clock.
And you can stand there with one small beer for an hour. Nobody moves you on. The table stays yours after you pay.
Count the places. The counter. The terrace. The station bar. The restaurant table. Two frames covered all four.
Nobody gave you those sentences. You made them on the spot, out of two openers you now own.
You will be served in one short sentence, with no 'sorry' in front of it. Most visitors spend a fortnight waiting to be noticed.
Shadowing. Out loud, with them, flat vowels, equal taps. The two that change every single day:

steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs OO-nah KAH-nyah, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Could I have a small draught beer, please?
Another one, please.
One more out loud, at a counter we have not stood at yet. A tray of small things with no name you know.

steps.promptPt: A bar up north, a tray behind glass, and you have no idea what any of them is called. Point at the good-looking one, and start. Speak now.
steps.es: ¿Me pones una de esas, por favor?
steps.pinyin: meh POH-nehs OO-nah deh EH-sahs, por fah-BOR
steps.pt: that one, there
steps.tts: ¿Me pones una de esas, por favor?

steps.pt: That is it. Greeted, served, seated, and you know what the seat costs. Next: the food itself. Hasta luego.

secoes.titulo: Why the terrace costs more — and when it stops being legal
secoes.corpo: Spanish consumer law lets a bar charge different amounts for the counter, the indoor tables and the terrace. What it does not let them do is spring it on you: the price list has to be displayed where a customer can see it, and the amounts shown must already include tax. So a terrace supplement that appears on the posted list is legal and there is nothing to argue about. One that appears only on the bill is a different matter, and that is what the complaint form later in the course is built for. The gap per drink is small; it is the fortnight, three drinks a day and two of you that makes it stop being small. We have deliberately not put a number on it — there is no published series for it, only anecdote.

exemplos.es: ¿Es el mismo precio en la terraza?
exemplos.pt: es el MEES-moh PREH-thyoh en lah teh-RRAH-thah — Is it the same price on the terrace?

exemplos.es: ¿Me deja ver la carta en papel, por favor?
exemplos.pt: meh DEH-khah behr lah KAR-tah en pah-PEL — Could I see a paper menu, please? (a QR code cannot be the only menu)

secoes.corpo: A 'caña' is a small glass of draught beer, served cold and drunk fast, which is the entire point. Order 'a beer' in English and you get a bottle, which costs more and goes warm. Other sizes on the board: a 'doble' is twice a caña; a 'tercio' is a 330ml bottle; and a 'jarra' of beer is a big glass, while a 'jarra de agua' is the jug for the middle of the table — same word, two objects, and the one after it tells you which. For wine, 'tinto' is red, 'blanco' white, 'rosado' rosé, and in some regions a small glass of red is a 'chato' or a 'corto'. A 'clara' is beer with lemonade, and it is not embarrassing in August. All of them slot into the same frame: ¿Me pones un tercio? ¿Me pones una clara? Nothing else in the sentence moves.

exemplos.pt: meh POH-nehs oon TEHR-thyoh — Could I have a bottle of beer, please?
OH-trah RROHN-dah — Another round, please. (the second frame, with the round on the end)

secoes.titulo: Free water, paid bread, and the free tapa that is only free in some places
secoes.corpo: The water is the cleanest right you have on this trip: since Ley 7/2022 came into force, hospitality venues must always offer the possibility of drinking unpackaged water free of charge. It was written as an anti-plastic measure rather than a consumer one, but the effect is identical. Ask for a 'jarra' rather than a glass — same law, enough for the table, one trip for the waiter. Bread, ice and the milk in your coffee are all things a bar may legitimately charge for, provided you were told beforehand or it is on the posted list; the offence is almost never the charge itself, it is the surprise. Which is why 'is it on the list?' is a more useful question than 'is this allowed?'. And the free tapa is geography, not law: eastern Andalusia — Granada above all, where a different plate comes with every round — plus Almería, where you pick from a list, and parts of Castilla y León and Galicia. Barcelona, Madrid, San Sebastián and Valencia treat the plate as an item you are buying. The Basque Country runs a third system: pintxos sit out on the counter, you help yourself, and the cocktail sticks left on your plate are what gets added up, so do not tidy them away.

exemplos.es: Una jarra de agua del grifo, por favor.
exemplos.pt: OO-nah KHAH-rrah deh AH-gwah del GREE-foh — A jug of tap water, please.
KWAN-tohs pah-LEE-yohs TYEH-nehs — 👂 'How many sticks have you got?' — he is not accusing you of anything, he is adding up.

secoes.corpo: Typically: breakfast is coffee and toast between half seven and nine; a second coffee around eleven; the main meal of the day, 'la comida', runs from two until about half three; a snack, 'la merienda', around five or six; and dinner, 'la cena', from nine, with kitchens taking last orders around half eleven. None of this is a rule and none of it is official — it is what most of the country happens to do, and the full version of it is a part of its own later in the course. The practical consequence is the one that matters now: a place happily serving full dinners at seven in the evening is, almost by definition, a place that lives on visitors, and that is where the inflated bill and the price-free 'tourist menu' live too. Eating at the local hour is not authenticity theatre. It is a filter.

exemplos.pt: ah keh OH-rah AH-breh lah koh-THEE-nah — What time does the kitchen open?
